question.problem:
Consider the polar curve $r={cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in [0,\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ),
$$

and ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\infty $

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$
question.worked_solution:
For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-3\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{+},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{\cancel{cos}\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{\cancel{2}}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}) \\  & =\frac{0-2\cdot 1}{-3\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{-}} \\  & =\frac{-2}{{0}^{+}} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Using the calculations from part II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}) \\  & =\frac{0-2\cdot 1}{-3\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{+}} \\  & =\frac{-2}{{0}^{-}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249911/assets/50637a502a56fc242ba5d8e2fda59ddc899295d4b14f7ae692869536b95ef661.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."
